subject: english
passage:
Dear Iris, I spent Friday with a family in Sweden during Midsummer, a celebration held in June. When we arrived at the village green, a long pole lay on the grass beside piles of leaves and flowers. Several neighbors were still tying plants to its wooden frame. __1__ By the time it stood upright, even my awkward contributions had become part of the display.
Once the music started, people formed a circle around the decorated pole. I remained at the edge, expecting to watch skilled local dancers. Then my host took my hand. __2__ She repeated the movements slowly, and I copied the people beside me. The children made mistakes too, but nobody seemed concerned about producing a perfect performance for visitors.
Later, we shared potatoes and strawberries at a long outdoor table. I went inside to fetch a jacket. __3__ It was already late in the evening, although the garden still looked bright. The long daylight around late June had confused my usual sense of an evening's progress. Outside, no one seemed in a hurry to end the conversation.
Before the visit, I had wondered what the celebration offered to people who disliked dancing. __4__ A quiet neighbor who had stayed outside the circle now passed dishes around and told me about the village. His part in the occasion was different from my host's, but just as welcoming. My photographs show flowers and dancers; they cannot fully show the conversations that made me feel at home. Love, Nina.

passage:
Monday. I agreed to play piano for a short silent film at our arts club. I had expected to learn one cheerful tune and repeat it. Learning the notes was only the beginning of preparing the music.
Tuesday. When the door opened, I could begin a new musical phrase. I no longer had to rush my playing to meet a time written in my notes.
Wednesday. At first I tried to answer every movement with a sound. Each step received a note, and each falling object received a crash. Friday. During the screening, the audience laughed longer than I had expected at one scene. subject: english
passage:
For this shadow theater workshop, you will use flat animals cut from thick black card. Place a small lamp behind a thin white screen, with a figure between the two. Before spending time on decoration, switch on the lamp and walk around to the front. __1__ Details that seem clear on your desk may disappear through the cloth. Judge the shape that reaches the audience, rather than the object in your hand.
Now compare a wolf and a dog. Their painted colors may differ, but their shadows can look almost identical. __2__ A longer nose or a differently shaped ear can help. Adding red paint to one animal will not help here: the thick card blocks the light, so the painted color never reaches the screen.
Next, make the wolf appear to grow while the dog stays small. Keep the lamp fixed, since moving it changes both shadows. You could cut a second wolf from a larger piece of card. __3__ Bring it closer to the lamp while the dog remains near the screen. The shadow grows without a change to the card. Return it toward the cloth to make its shadow small again.
Finally, watch for a third character that nobody intended to create. It may arrive when a performer reaches across the beam to adjust a figure. __4__ This human shape can briefly hide both animals. Keep spare card and tools behind the lamp, and practice moving the animals without crossing your arms through the light. An empty screen can reveal these unwanted shapes before they interrupt the play.
q: __1__ 處最適合填入哪一個句子？
choices: Yet you can achieve this effect with the figure you have.
A hand in the light can cast a shadow of its own.
Their outlines must carry the difference between them.
Moving both figures together can suggest a journey shared by the two animals.
This first check compares the figure with its shadow.
explain: first check（初次檢查）回指開燈並走到布幕正面，後文比較實物與影像的細節。「用現有紙偶達到效果」尚無放大影子的目標可供回指。

subject: english
passage:
Dear Leo, yesterday's village tour began with an argument about a shortcut. Our guide, Maya, turned away from the narrow lane shown in the visitor brochure. Several people complained that her route would take longer. __1__ An open gate, she explained, did not make that space a public path.
Maya did not avoid all residential streets. The houses were still in daily use, with bicycles by the doors and washing hanging from the windows. When we paused to hear about their history, she noticed that our group was blocking several entrances. __2__ Moments later, a woman came out carrying a large basket. She thanked us for keeping the way open.
Later, we stopped beside a house with a beautifully painted doorway. Several group members reached for their phones. __3__ One man agreed to a portrait but asked us not to include the inside of his home. Maya respected both parts of his answer and waited until he stepped outside.
The walk ended in a small public square rather than at a souvenir shop. Nobody had been pushed to buy anything, and we had seen fewer sights than promised in the brochure. __4__ We had learned how to be visitors without treating every home as part of an attraction. I would gladly join another walk led by someone who knew when to keep a respectful distance.
q: __1__ 處最適合填入哪一個句子？
choices: She checked whether anyone there wished to be photographed.
Maya had chosen the route because these homes were no longer occupied.
The shortcut crossed a yard that belonged to a family.
Even so, I came away with a deeper sense of the place.
We moved aside to leave a clear route to each door.
explain: 前文抱怨繞路，後文的 that space（那個空間）須回指私人院子，才說得通開門不等於公共通道。空屋句未交代院子，且與後文居民仍住在屋內矛盾。

Field notes, Monday. Our old aerial photograph seemed to place the river bend too close to a barn. At the site, the barn and the road matched the picture, but the bend lay farther away. A date on the back showed that the photograph had been taken twenty years earlier. __1__ We decided to test this possibility by looking for signs of change along the banks.
From a high footpath, we saw exposed roots hanging over the outside of one bend. Fresh pieces of earth lay in the water below. __2__ Across the river, however, a low patch of sand extended gently into the channel. No construction work had been done on either bank.
The sand on the inner bank offered a different clue. __3__ In other words, one side of the bend was receiving material while the other was losing it. Together, these processes could explain why the old photograph no longer matched the river's present position.
We measured the distance from a stone post to the bank and photographed the bend from the footpath. __4__ A view taken from a different spot could make the bank look farther away even if it had not moved. The same viewpoint would make future comparisons more reliable.
Our afternoon's observations did not tell us how quickly the whole river was changing. For that, we would need records from more places and more dates. We had nevertheless learned to read a riverbank as evidence of movement rather than as a fixed line in the landscape.
q: __1__ 處最適合填入哪一個句子？
choices: The slower water there let the sand it carried settle.
The river might have moved even though the road and barn had not.
Perhaps the barn had been rebuilt farther from the river since the photo was taken.
The current was carrying soil away from that outer bank.
We marked our camera position for the next visit.
explain: 道路與穀倉仍對得上，河彎卻不同，舊照又相隔二十年，故推測河道移動。move（移動）是核心概念；穀倉移位說違反地標與舊照吻合的線索，接不上待驗證的 possibility（可能性）。

To the school board: After evening practice, our sports club walks through grounds that shine long after most students leave. Some lamps send light into the sky and neighboring windows. __1__ Those gaps force walkers to slow down near the steps. Clearly, a bright view from a distance does not guarantee useful light under our feet.
The first change should concern direction rather than brightness. __2__ Their purpose would be to keep light on the walking surface instead of sending it beyond the school fence. Before purchasing stronger bulbs, we should examine where the existing light actually falls and adjust the lamps accordingly.
Direction, however, is only part of the problem. The grounds remain lit until midnight, although the last activity usually finishes much earlier. __3__ A timer could switch off lamps in empty areas after the grounds close, while staff could adjust the setting for special evening events.

The school could also compare electricity used before and during the trial, taking any special events into account.
If the trial reveals a dark corner, the arrangement should be corrected before it becomes permanent. The aim is to provide light where and when it serves a purpose. With a careful trial, the school can protect its evening users while reducing unnecessary light beyond its grounds.
q: __1__ 處最適合填入哪一個句子？

The operating hours should reflect when people need light.

Yet several parts of the path still lie in deep shadow.

Museum audio guide: A bowl of fruit may look out of place in a display about sea travel. Yet it points to an important episode in medical testing. In 1747, James Lind, a ship's doctor, studied twelve sailors with scurvy, a disease that could make them terribly weak. __1__ Two received oranges and lemons; the other pairs received different treatments.
The sailors shared the same basic diet and stayed in the same part of the ship. __2__ If one pair had enjoyed better meals or different living conditions, an improvement might have been wrongly credited to its treatment. A fair comparison required attention to more than the medicine itself.
The men given fruit showed a striking improvement within days. This was valuable evidence that oranges and lemons could help. __3__ The comparison did not identify the substance in the fruit responsible for the improvement. Finding a treatment that worked and understanding why it worked were separate steps.
Nor did the result immediately transform meals throughout the navy. Keeping fruit juice usable on long voyages was one practical difficulty. __4__ By then, several decades had passed since the small shipboard comparison. The long gap warns us against imagining that a promising finding changes everyday practice at once.
As you leave, think about why the fruit belongs in this exhibition. It represents more than a useful food. The display asks us to notice the comparison behind a medical claim, the limits of what that comparison can establish, and the distance between evidence and its widespread use.
q: __1__ 處最適合填入哪一個句子？
choices: He assigned a different treatment to each pair of men.
These shared conditions helped make the comparison fair.
In 1795, the navy approved regular supplies of lemon juice.
Yet success in treatment left another question unanswered.
The improvement showed that the fruit's active substance had been identified.
explain: 後文分述吃水果的兩人與其餘各組，須先建立 pair（兩人一組）及不同處置的架構。共同條件句此時沒有飲食、住處可回指；辨出有效物質也不是分組依據。

Reporter: Why would a health laboratory study water from toilets? Scientist: People infected with certain viruses can leave traces of those viruses in their waste. We collect water arriving at a treatment plant before it is cleaned. Toilets across the district feed into that same system. __1__ This broad coverage is useful when people have mild symptoms or choose to recover at home.
Reporter: What can a reading tell you about the people it represents? Scientist: Infected people release different amounts of virus, and the amount can change during an infection. Extra water entering the system can also make a sample weaker. __2__ So we focus on changes over time rather than announcing how many residents are ill.
Reporter: How do you follow those changes? Scientist: We collect samples regularly at the same location and use a consistent method. Friday's result may be higher than Monday's. __3__ A rise lasting through several collections gives us greater confidence that the broader pattern has changed.
Reporter: Where do hospital figures fit into this picture? Scientist: __4__ They tell us, for example, how many beds are occupied. Individual tests can also confirm infections. Together, these sources provide a fuller picture than any single method can offer.
Reporter: What should the public take from this? Scientist: Think of the system as a way to watch changes across a community. It can help health services prepare for growing demand, but it cannot give any particular resident a diagnosis. Its usefulness depends on asking questions that the evidence can actually answer.
q: __1__ 處最適合填入哪一個句子？
choices: The samples can show which homes contain people carrying the virus.
But one change is not enough to establish a trend.
Samples can include traces from people who skip testing.
Medical reports fill gaps left by the water samples.
Those differences prevent an exact count of sick people.

An apple can look different only minutes after it is sliced. The pale surface gradually turns brown, even though the whole fruit looked unchanged for days. What has the knife done? Cutting damages cells, allowing substances that were kept apart to mix. An enzyme, a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction, helps these substances react with oxygen from the air. Brown compounds then appear on the exposed surface.
This explanation suggests several ways to slow the change. Lemon juice makes the surface more acidic, reducing the activity of the enzyme. Covering the slices with water limits their contact with air. These approaches affect different parts of the process, although both can help the slices keep their pale appearance for a while.
For a school food display, a class placed equal slices from one apple in three dishes. One group received lemon juice, another remained under water, and the third was left uncovered. All three stayed in the same room and were checked at the same times. The uncovered pieces darkened fastest. However, when classmates tasted the treated pieces, some disliked the sour flavor of the lemon group, while others preferred its stronger taste. The class therefore chose to display both the color observations and the taste comments. A successful treatment, they concluded, depended partly on what the fruit would be used for.
q: Which title best covers the three paragraphs?
choices: Why Cutting an Apple Changes Its Color
Keeping Apple Slices Pale: Methods and Choices
Lemon Juice: The Class's Favorite Treatment
Comparing the Flavors of Different Apples
explain: 全文從褐變機制談到處理方法及口味取捨，須選涵蓋這些內容的標題。pale 是「淡色的」；只談切開後變色的原因，會漏掉後兩段的處理與選擇。

Cutting damages cells, allowing substances that were kept apart to mix. An enzyme, a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction, helps these substances react with oxygen from the air. Brown compounds then appear on the exposed surface.
This explanation suggests several ways to slow the change. Lemon juice makes the surface more acidic, reducing the activity of the enzyme. Covering the slices with water limits their contact with air. These approaches affect different parts of the process, although both can help the slices keep their pale appearance for a while.
For a school food display, a class placed equal slices from one apple in three dishes. One group received lemon juice, another remained under water, and the third was left uncovered. All three stayed in the same room and were checked at the same times. The uncovered pieces darkened fastest. However, when classmates tasted the treated pieces, some disliked the sour flavor of the lemon group, while others preferred its stronger taste. The class therefore chose to display both the color observations and the taste comments. A successful treatment, they concluded, depended partly on what the fruit would be used for.
q: What does water do in the process described?
choices: It makes the surface more acidic than lemon does.
It reduces the slices' contact with air.
It separates the substances inside damaged cells.
It speeds up the reaction that changes the color.
explain: 第二段說水限制切片接觸空氣。contact 是「接觸」；提高酸性是檸檬汁的作用，不能套在水上。

Dear June, You asked why I planted another crop after selling the last vegetables of the season. You expected to see an empty field when you visited. The new green plants are a cover crop. I am growing them mainly to protect the ground between harvests, rather than to sell another load of food.
An empty field may look tidy, but its soil is open to wind and rain. A cover crop softens the force of falling drops, and its roots help hold soil in place. When the plants are cut and left on the surface, their remains can continue to shield the ground. The crop is doing useful work even when no truck comes to collect it. In that sense, this quiet field is still part of my business.
There is a cost, of course. I buy seeds and spend time planting them. Living plants also use water, so I must decide when to stop their growth. In a dry spring, leaving them alive too long could mean less water for the vegetables I plan to grow next. That decision depends on local conditions, not just on how green the field looks.
I have started with one section so I can compare its costs and condition with the rest. If you visit next month, bring your notebook. I would like help recording what we find, including any problems. I want a useful record, not simply a photograph that makes my farm look responsible. Best, Uncle Ben
q: What is Ben chiefly trying to explain to June?
choices: How he plans to promote his farm to visitors
Why he grows plants he does not plan to sell
Why he sells vegetables before the dry season
How he will turn his whole farm into a garden
explain: 開頭的疑問與後文效益、成本都在解釋不販售的種植。cover crop 是「覆蓋作物」；拍照宣傳反而是信末不願只做的事。

A comet made Maria Mitchell famous, but a telescope was only one of the tools that shaped her life. Born on the American island of Nantucket in 1818, she learned mathematics and sky observation with her father. She later worked as a librarian. During quiet hours at the library, she continued studying subjects that interested her. Books and the night sky offered different ways to pursue the same curiosity.
In 1847, Mitchell spotted a comet through a telescope. The discovery brought her international attention and a gold medal from the king of Denmark. It could have become the single event by which she was remembered. Yet her later work extended beyond identifying an unfamiliar object in the sky. In 1865, she became a professor of astronomy at Vassar, a college established to educate women.
There, students took part in research rather than merely reading about other people's findings. They observed the sky, made records, and joined trips to watch solar eclipses, when the Moon blocks the Sun. Mitchell published student observations alongside her own work. The young women were being treated as contributors to knowledge, not just receivers of it.
Seen together, the library, the comet, and the classroom show a career with more than one center. Mitchell gained recognition through a discovery, then helped other women gain direct experience in science. Her story invites us to measure a scientist's influence partly by the opportunities she creates for others.
q: Which description best captures the focus of this account?
choices: A librarian who left books behind for sky study
An observer whose success depended on one award
A scientist whose influence included her students
A professor who replaced research with teaching
explain: 全文由自學、發現到帶學生研究，強調影響也包含培育他人。influence 是「影響」；她並未用教學取代研究。

subject: english
passage:
Welcome to the final room of our introduction to Henri Matisse. The French artist spent much of his career exploring color through painting. In his later years, he gave scissors a central role in that exploration. The works known as his cut-outs might look simple at first: flat shapes placed beside or over one another. Their apparent ease, however, hides an active process of choice and revision.
Matisse did not generally begin with ready-made colored paper. Assistants covered white sheets with paint, creating a supply of colors for him to choose from. He cut shapes from these sheets, joining the making of a line with the selection of a colored area. For small works, he could arrange the pieces on a board. For large ones, assistants placed them on the studio walls according to his directions. The wall became a working surface, not merely somewhere to hang a finished picture.
Pins were important to this method. Before the pieces were fixed permanently, their positions could be changed. A shape could move upward, a gap could widen, or two colors could become neighbors. The arrangement remained open to revision as Matisse examined its effect. A finished work records one chosen relationship among many that were possible.
As you leave, imagine the room before the arrangement was settled. Think of pieces being shifted and reconsidered. This imagined movement can help you see the finished work as the outcome of decisions, rather than as a pattern produced in one effortless moment.
q: What does the guide most want visitors to appreciate?
choices: The benefits of using paper instead of paint
The division of work among studio assistants
The reasons for making larger works later in life
explain: 首段指出簡單外觀下的反覆修改，末段再請觀眾想像選擇過程。revision 是「修改」；助手分工只是部分內容，不能概括全文要觀眾體會的創作抉擇。

The photograph seems to show a jumper doing things the wrong way around. His back faces the bar, and his head crosses it before his feet. At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, American athlete Dick Fosbury won the high jump with this unusual style. To viewers unfamiliar with him, the method could have looked like a sudden invention made for the occasion.
Its development had actually begun years earlier. As a high school student, Fosbury struggled with the widely taught method in which athletes crossed the bar facing downward. Instead of simply repeating an approach that was not working for him, he experimented with his body position. Over time, his backward jump became effective enough to carry him into major competitions. The Olympic audience saw the result of that development, rather than its beginning.
The surroundings of the sport mattered too. Softer foam landing areas were becoming available, making a landing on the back much safer than it would have been in older sand or sawdust landing pits. Fosbury was not the only athlete exploring backward jumping. Canadian jumper Debbie Brill was also developing a similar approach. Individual experiments and changes in equipment were moving together.
After Fosbury's Olympic victory, the technique he called the Fosbury flop spread widely. The gold medal provided a public demonstration that an unfamiliar technique could succeed. Yet reducing the story to one winning afternoon misses much of what made that afternoon possible: repeated adjustments, suitable equipment, and a willingness to question a familiar way of moving.
q: Which theme links the stages of Fosbury's story?
choices: How safer equipment changed high-jump landings
How a new jumping style developed and spread
Why an Olympic victory requires years of training
Why two athletes used the same backward technique
explain: 全文串起早期試驗、器材與奪冠後普及，重點是新跳法如何發展及傳播。technique 是「技術」；落地設備雖重要，卻只是促成變革的一個因素。

The photograph seems to show a jumper doing things the wrong way around. His back faces the bar, and his head crosses it before his feet. At the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, American athlete Dick Fosbury won the high jump with this unusual style. To viewers unfamiliar with him, the method could have looked like a sudden invention made for the occasion.
Its development had actually begun years earlier. As a high school student, Fosbury struggled with the widely taught method in which athletes crossed the bar facing downward. Instead of simply repeating an approach that was not working for him, he experimented with his body position. Over time, his backward jump became effective enough to carry him into major competitions. The Olympic audience saw the result of that development, rather than its beginning.
The surroundings of the sport mattered too. Softer foam landing areas were becoming available, making a landing on the back much safer than it would have been in older sand or sawdust landing pits. Fosbury was not the only athlete exploring backward jumping. Canadian jumper Debbie Brill was also developing a similar approach. Individual experiments and changes in equipment were moving together.
After Fosbury's Olympic victory, the technique he called the Fosbury flop spread widely. The gold medal provided a public demonstration that an unfamiliar technique could succeed. Yet reducing the story to one winning afternoon misses much of what made that afternoon possible: repeated adjustments, suitable equipment, and a willingness to question a familiar way of moving.

To explain why Brill competed in Mexico City
To trace the method's name to its Canadian roots
To place Fosbury's work within wider changes

Memo to the River News team: A rumor says the town's old market hall will be replaced with apartments. Three websites report it, and messages shared by residents cite "multiple reports" as confirmation. Our draft repeats that phrase. Before treating the number of articles as evidence, I traced where their information came from.
All three led back to one property agency's brochure. The first website quoted the brochure directly. The second summarized the first article, and the third copied that summary, including an error in the street name. The brochure described a possible project if the hall were sold; it did not announce an agreed sale. None of the websites had contacted the owner or the planning office. We had found several routes for the same claim to travel, rather than several separate checks of it.
The brochure may still provide a useful starting point. A commercial source can describe a real possibility, so dismissing it simply because an agency produced it would be careless too. We should ask the owner whether a sale has been agreed and the planning office whether an application has been submitted. Their answers could support, limit, or contradict the proposal. Until then, our headline should distinguish a proposed redevelopment from a confirmed decision. The repeated articles deserve investigation, but counting web addresses is no substitute for finding out what each report actually adds.
q: What is the writer chiefly asking the team to do?
choices: Check how many sources the reports really use.
Treat several reports as confirmation of a sale.
Reject the story because a business shared it first.
Compare the reports to choose the best-written one.

At the grocery store, I reached for the largest bag of flour. A bright label called it the "family value pack," and I assumed that more flour meant a better deal. My sister asked me to compare the small print on the shelf. Both sizes were from the same brand and contained the same kind of flour. The large bag cost less for each kilogram, although its total price was higher. I thought that settled the matter.
Then she asked how much I would use. I was buying flour for a few baking sessions while staying in a small apartment for a month. There was no spare cupboard, and I would leave by train when the visit ended. The small bag would cover my planned recipes. I could take it home easily if some remained, but carrying the large bag would be difficult. Buying more would make sense only if I found extra uses or someone willing to share it.
I chose the small bag. This did not make the shelf label false, nor did it make the larger size a bad purchase for everyone. For a household that baked frequently and had storage space, the larger bag could offer real savings. My mistake had been to treat a lower price per kilogram as a complete answer to a personal question. The useful comparison involved not just how cheaply I could obtain flour, but how much of it would actually serve a purpose.
q: Which lesson does the narrator draw from the purchase?
choices: A famous brand makes a large pack a good deal.
Smaller packs tend to cost less per kilogram.
A family label helps more than shelf details.
A good deal depends partly on what one can use.
explain: 結尾把單位價格與實際用途合看，才是好交易。deal 是「交易、划算的購買」；小包單位較便宜與第一段相反。

Reporter: You volunteer to describe local football matches for fans who cannot see the field clearly. Is it like reporting on the radio? Leah: There are similarities, but our listeners are sitting in the stadium. They already hear the crowd and feel the excitement. They need information about movements they cannot see. We lend them small receivers, so they can choose when to listen rather than hear our voices through loudspeakers.
Reporter: How do you decide what to include? Leah: Before a match, I learn the players' names and practice describing positions. During play, I put the location of the ball before comments about a player's style. Saying that a pass was wonderful tells listeners less than explaining where it went. A listener once asked me to stop calling every fast move amazing. She wanted enough information to judge it herself. Her advice changed my preparation.
Reporter: Does that mean you speak throughout the match? Leah: I leave pauses when nothing important is happening. Some fans want to talk with friends or enjoy the stadium sounds. The receivers let them do that. Afterward, I ask whether they could track the action, not whether they liked my voice. At our last practice, another volunteer described a recorded match while I listened without watching. I lost the ball within a minute. Now I understand how a clear voice can still leave a listener confused.
q: Which heading best expresses the central focus of this interview?
choices: Preparing a Clear Voice for a Crowded Stadium

Leah: There are similarities, but our listeners are sitting in the stadium. They already hear the crowd and feel the excitement. They need information about movements they cannot see. Now I understand how a clear voice can still leave a listener confused.

Describe players' styles before their movements.
Use longer descriptions during every break.
Make the ball's changing position easier to follow.

Dear Neighborhood Committee, I welcome the plan to let residents choose how part of our community budget is spent. However, the first vote should come after a period for improving the proposals. Otherwise, an attractive promise may win support before anyone checks whether it can be delivered.
Consider the two ideas discussed last week. The garden group wants lighting for evening work, while several parents want a covered waiting area outside the activity center. Both would require money after construction: lamps need electricity, and a roof needs maintenance. A proposal should therefore include its first year's running costs as well as its building costs. This would let voters weigh the full cost of each choice. Volunteers could help applicants prepare these estimates, but the same rules should apply to every group.
We also need to hear from residents who do not attend meetings. The current plan allows online voting for a week, which is convenient for many people. Yet some residents have no internet connection at home. A paper voting desk at the center would give them another way to take part. Posting a summary of each proposal there would also help people who missed the discussion.
These steps will take time. I suggest delaying the vote by two weeks, without changing the amount available. A shared budget deserves a process in which people can compare realistic choices and have a practical chance to express a preference. Sincerely, Dana Wu

Improve the process before residents vote.
Raise the budget for the proposed projects.

Teachers seeking a course in examination skills.

A city can depend on a route that no traveler can see on the ground. During the Berlin Airlift of 1948–1949, that route was in the sky. After the Second World War, Germany was divided into zones controlled by the victorious powers. Berlin, although located inside the Soviet zone, was also divided. This left the western parts of the city separated from the western zones of Germany.
In June 1948, the Soviet Union blocked road, rail, and water access from the west to those parts of Berlin. The Western Allies faced a difficult choice. Sending armed forces along the closed routes risked a direct conflict, while abandoning the city would leave its residents without vital supplies. The United States and Britain chose to use agreed air routes to carry in necessities. Food was essential, but so was coal, which provided energy for homes and industry.
Keeping the deliveries going required more than brave pilots. Aircraft had to arrive in a carefully managed sequence, and ground teams had to unload them quickly. Improvements in these routines helped the airlift carry growing amounts of cargo. The operation thus depended on people working at both ends of a journey, not simply on the number of planes available.
The blockade ended in 1949, but supply flights continued for a time afterward. The airlift did not remove the political division of Berlin. It demonstrated that a vast transport operation could sustain a city through a crisis without forcing open the blocked ground routes.
q: Which title best covers the account?
choices: Reopening Berlin's Ground Routes by Force
The Role of Coal in Berlin's Recovery
Keeping a Divided City Supplied by Air
The Pilots Who Ended Berlin's Political Division
explain: 全文涵蓋封鎖背景、空運選擇及補給運作；煤只是物資之一，空運也未消除政治分裂。supply＝供應。

Welcome to this stop on our journey through archaeological discoveries. Today, imagine looking down into a long hollow in the soil. It is shaped like a boat, yet there is no wooden boat to lift out. This was the remarkable situation faced by the team uncovering a burial at Sutton Hoo in England in 1939.
The wood had decayed long before the discovery. However, the soil preserved an impression of the ship, and iron pieces that had fastened its boards together remained. Their positions helped reveal its construction. The discovery therefore depended on recognizing relationships among small remains and changes in the ground, rather than simply finding an object that still looked complete.
Inside the ship's outline was a burial chamber containing richly made objects, including weapons and gold decorations. These finds showed exceptional skill and connections with places beyond England. They helped challenge an older picture of early England as a place with little artistic achievement or contact with the wider world. Yet impressive objects cannot answer every question. The identity of the person buried there is still debated; a rich burial does not come with a name attached.
As you continue, keep two questions separate: what has survived, and what can be learned from it? At Sutton Hoo, much of the ship itself was gone, but evidence of its form remained. The costly objects offered another kind of evidence, about status and wider connections. Archaeology draws on both, while leaving room for questions that the available material cannot settle.
q: What is the speaker's main aim in this talk?
choices: To argue that rich objects provide the best evidence
To explain how researchers identified a buried ruler
To outline how a buried wooden ship was restored
To explain how surviving clues reveal the past
explain: 船形痕跡與物件提供不同線索，全文引導讀者理解如何據此認識過去；沒有主張貴重物品的證據價值最高。remains＝遺存。

A closed road can look like an unnecessary delay when the rain has stopped. A driver may recognize the route, see a vehicle on the far side, and decide that officials have been too cautious. Yet a familiar road under floodwater is no longer a familiar driving surface. The visible water tells only part of its story.
Water can hide a section where the road has been damaged or washed away. Its depth may also be difficult to judge from the bank. A driver who remembers the road as flat is relying on information about yesterday's road, not its present condition. Similarly, seeing another car reach the other side does not reveal what will happen to the next vehicle as conditions change.
It is easy to underestimate this danger when the alternative route is long. Using a longer route creates an immediate, certain cost in time, whereas the risk of crossing may feel distant and uncertain. That difference can make the risky choice seem reasonable. But the length of an alternative route supplies no evidence about the safety of the flooded section. Neither does the driver's wish to get home quickly.
Road barriers should therefore be treated as boundaries, not invitations to conduct a personal test. Follow current official information and use an open route instead. Communities can make this choice easier by providing clear directions for the alternative. A good warning does more than announce danger: it helps people act on that information without asking them to judge what they cannot see.
q: Which title best captures the writer's argument?
choices: How a Longer Route Affects a Driver's Decision

Dear Alex, you asked why our coastal field trip included a walk up a hill before we visited the beach. Finding the signs on a calm morning was much easier than looking for them during an emergency.
At the beach, the guide asked us to imagine that the sea suddenly pulled back, exposing ground that would normally be underwater. Several students said they would want a photograph. She explained that this could be a natural warning of a tsunami, a series of powerful ocean waves. A strong or long earthquake near the coast is another warning. After protecting ourselves during shaking, we should move toward safety as soon as it is safe to do so. Waiting beside the water for a message on a phone could waste valuable time.
Later, at the safe meeting point above the coast, she asked what we would do if a first wave arrived and the water then became quiet. I said we could probably return for our bags. She shook her head. A tsunami can include several waves, and the first may not be the largest. We should stay outside the danger area until local officials say we can return.
I had expected a lesson in watching the ocean. Instead, I learned when to leave it behind. We still took photographs that afternoon, but the most useful thing I brought home was a clear idea of where to go. Best, Mina

A page covered with corrections can look like evidence of hard work. Yet copying every correct answer into a notebook may leave a student unable to explain the next mistake. A useful mistake notebook records a decision that went wrong, not simply the answer that should replace it.
Consider two students who choose the wrong answer to a reading question. One does not know a word in the question. The other understands every word but selects a statement that is true of one paragraph rather than the whole passage. Writing "read more carefully" beside both errors hides the difference. Dear Aunt May, Your message asked whether Leo and I would join the school drama club together. I laughed because the club leader asked me the same thing. Being twins seems to make people expect a single answer from us, even when our interests lead us in different directions.

Neither of us joined the other's club, but each discovered work behind the other's interest.
So please come to Leo's play if he gets a part. I may be in the audience, and I may write about it afterward. That would not mean I had finally become interested in acting myself. We still share plenty of stories; we are simply learning that sharing a life does not require giving the same reply. Love, Nina.
q: Which heading would suit Nina's letter best?
choices: Two Clubs Competing for New Members
A Family Learning to Perform Together
From Taking Pictures to Becoming an Actor
Close as Twins, Different in Choice

Reporter: You recently misread a writer's message. What happened? Editor: I suggested a new title for Ana's story. She replied, "Fine." I remembered a disagreement from the day before and assumed she was angry. I began writing a long defense of my choice. Fortunately, she came into the office before I sent it.
Reporter: Was she angry? Editor: No. She had been standing on a crowded bus, trying to hold a bag and her phone. She liked the title and had sent the shortest reply she could manage. I had treated the missing explanation as evidence of dislike. The message told me her decision, but I had invented the feeling behind it.
Reporter: Would using more cheerful words solve this? Editor: Sometimes extra words help, but I would not ask everyone to decorate every reply. Ana should be able to send a quick answer. Now, when the meaning matters, I ask a specific question before reacting. I also state my own purpose more clearly. If I need approval rather than a fresh suggestion, I say so. Otherwise, a helpful alternative can seem like an unwanted change.

That does not mean ignoring a clear objection. It means separating what the person wrote from the story you added. We still disagree about titles, but at least we now discuss the title instead of an emotion neither of us actually expressed.

choices: A mistake leads to reflection and new habits.
Two editors debate the value of shorter messages.
A vague title is revised through team discussions.
A writer's refusal leads to a defense of the title.

At a neighborhood food fair, one stall offered a dish called "Grandmother's Sunday." Visitors smiled at the name but kept asking what they would actually receive. The dish was a bowl of noodles with vegetables, named after the stall owner's childhood visits. Its title carried a family memory, not a list of ingredients.
The fair's organizers had first asked every cook for a direct English translation of a dish's name. They thought this would make the menus equally clear. In practice, some translated names described a cooking method, while others referred to a person, place, or family joke. Equal treatment of the names did not give visitors equally useful information. Changing "Grandmother's Sunday" to "Noodles," however, would have removed the story that made the cook eager to share it.
The organizers settled on a new label design. A short description stated the main ingredients and how the food was prepared. Beneath it, the cook could explain the name in a sentence. The original name remained at the top. Visitors could decide what to order without requiring a family story to do the work of an ingredient list. Those interested in the story could ask more.
The labels were also personal. One cook's version was described as the one her family made, rather than the dish everyone from her hometown ate. A menu can reflect a person's experience without standing for a whole community. By closing time, the organizers had learned that making food easier to understand did not require making every name sound familiar.
q: Why does the writer begin with "Grandmother's Sunday"?
choices: To show why a dish's name can need explanation.
To suggest that personal names make menus clearer.
To show that translation should replace family memories.
To argue that ingredient lists can explain family ties.

Our student shop has begun selling imported snacks with American Nutrition Facts labels. Some shoppers look for the smallest calorie number and stop reading there. I welcome the interest in labels, but a number is useful only when we know the quantity of food it describes. Without that quantity, an apparently simple comparison can become misleading.
The figures on these labels usually describe one serving, although some packages also provide figures for the entire contents. A serving is not necessarily the whole bag. Imagine two snacks whose labels each list calories for one serving. If those servings differ in weight, the displayed numbers do not compare equal amounts of food. A smaller number might simply go with a smaller amount. Comparing the same weight gives the numbers a common basis.
There is another reason to notice serving information. Under the American labeling system, serving sizes reflect amounts people commonly consume; they are not instructions about what each reader ought to eat. Treating a label as a personal meal plan gives it a job it was not designed to perform. Nor does finding fewer calories settle every question about a food. The label contains other information, and a snack is only part of what someone eats.
I propose a small sign beside the shop's shelves: "What amount does that number describe?" Staff could use empty packages to show both a serving and a whole package. The aim would be to help students interpret information, rather than to rank shoppers by what they buy or turn a single figure into a complete judgment.

Monday. Maya told me she had signed up to help at an animal shelter on Saturdays. For two years, Saturday had meant our trip to the used-book market. We rarely bought anything, but we knew which stall would have something strange to show each other. I congratulated her, then spent the afternoon wondering whether we had begun to drift apart.
Tuesday. I wrote an angry message: "You have time for everyone except me." Before sending it, I checked my calendar. Maya had suggested meeting on Wednesday, but I had refused because of my evening art course. I had not considered missing that class to see her. Somehow, my own new interest had seemed like part of growing up, while hers had felt like a decision against our friendship. I deleted the message.
Friday. We talked after school. Maya said she missed the market too, but wanted to keep volunteering. I admitted that I wanted to continue my course. We chose the first Sunday of each month for a visit to the market. We would meet less often, and neither of us could promise every Sunday forever. Still, it was a plan we both wanted, rather than one either accepted out of guilt.
Sunday. Maya described a dog that refused to leave its blanket, and I showed her a drawing I had struggled to finish. Neither story would have existed during our old Saturdays. The afternoon felt familiar without being a copy of the past. Our favorite market stall had changed its display, and, for once, I did not wish it had stayed exactly the same.
q: What change does this journal mainly record?
choices: Discovering why an old meeting place loses its appeal.
Choosing between an art course and volunteer work.
Learning to accept a friendship's altered routine.
Replacing a market visit with work at a shelter.
explain: 由擔心疏遠，到接受新相處節奏，routine（固定活動）可變而情誼仍在；兩人保留各自活動，並未在課程與志工間二選一。

A dancer holding a still pose may appear to be doing nothing. In fact, the brain is receiving information and making small corrections. Balance depends on more than strong muscles. The eyes provide information about the surroundings, the inner ears report movements and the position of the head, and signals from muscles and joints help the brain track the body's position. These sources work together rather than taking turns.
A simple demonstration makes their cooperation easier to notice. Imagine standing comfortably beside a firm support, first looking straight ahead and then closing your eyes. Some people notice more movement with their eyes shut. This does not mean that the balance system has stopped working. One source of information has become unavailable, while the others remain active. A firm floor also provides a different situation from a soft surface that shifts beneath the feet. Changing several conditions together would make the result harder to interpret.
The demonstration is sometimes treated as a contest: whoever moves least must have the best balance. That conclusion goes beyond what a brief activity can show. People begin with different experience, and a single observation tells little about how they move in daily life. A more useful question is what changes when one condition changes. Seen this way, the dancer's stillness is not an absence of activity. It is the visible outcome of continuous communication, most of which the audience never notices.
q: What central idea does the explanation develop?
choices: Strong muscles can take the place of other signals.
Keeping still depends on several signal sources.
A brief test shows who has the best daily balance.
Removing visual input improves balance control.
explain: 開頭列出多種訊號，結尾以持續溝通解釋站穩。balance＝平衡。閉眼活動只顯示條件改變的影響，不能代表日常能力。

Class project report: Predicting a disappointing afternoon. Before a puzzle tournament, twenty-eight volunteers in our psychology class predicted how upset they would feel if their team lost. We asked for separate ratings for the end of the game, thirty minutes later, and one hour later. After the tournament, those whose teams had lost supplied actual ratings at those same points. Winners' ratings were kept separate because they had not experienced the outcome in our question.
The losing players' first ratings were close to their predictions. Over the next hour, however, their disappointment faded more quickly than they had expected. Brief interviews offered a possible explanation. Before playing, students had pictured the loss in detail. Afterwards, their afternoon also contained a snack, conversations, and plans for the weekend. The game had not become unimportant, but it occupied less of their attention than it had in the imagined afternoon.
Our report therefore separates a reasonable observation from an attractive claim. These students overestimated how long their disappointment would last after this particular game. We cannot conclude that people recover quickly from every kind of loss. Nor did we assign different afternoon activities to different groups, so the interviews do not establish which activity changed anyone's feelings. For a follow-up, we would like half the volunteers to describe an ordinary hour after the game before making predictions. Comparing their forecasts with those of the other half could help us examine whether including everyday events makes a difference.
q: Which heading would suit the entire report?
choices: Why Players Expected a Longer Tournament
A Gap Between Expected and Reported Disappointment
The Role of Weekend Plans in Team Performance

subject: english
passage:
Our town's promise to plant five hundred trees sounds encouraging. Yet the number alone tells us little about what a walk across town will feel like. A tree shades the ground beneath its branches, not every street in the same neighborhood. If new trees are concentrated around the riverside park while the route to the market remains exposed, residents carrying groceries will see little immediate difference on that journey.
Last week, our neighborhood group walked two possible routes from the apartments to the market at noon. The riverside route already had shade but required a long detour. The direct route had young trees surrounded by small openings in the pavement. They may provide useful shade eventually, but walkers cannot count on that protection this summer. Several older residents therefore chose the long route despite the extra distance. Their decisions suggest that a pleasant park and a comfortable daily journey are related goals, but they are not interchangeable.
We support planting more trees. We also ask the town to show where their shade will fall, how much space they have to grow, and who will care for them. For stretches where trees cannot yet provide cover, temporary shade structures deserve consideration. Before celebrating a total on a poster, officials should walk the routes at the times people use them. Counting trunks is straightforward. Understanding whether residents can reach shops, schools, and bus stops comfortably takes more attention, but that is the outcome the investment should serve.
q: Which statement best expresses the editorial's position?
choices: Riverside parks should receive most of the new trees.
Walkers should adapt their routes to existing shade.
Shade plans should fit people's daily journeys.
Planting totals are the best measure of useful shade.
explain: 作者要求檢查居民實際使用的路線、時段與遮蔭，並考慮暫時設施。shade＝遮蔭；不是要行人遷就現有樹蔭，也不能用種植總數取代舒適通行的成效。

Interviewer: The new hall looked beautiful when it opened. Why did you return with heavy curtains? Architect: At the first public meeting, people at the back could hear the speaker's voice but struggled to understand the words. Hard surfaces reflected sound around the room. Parts of earlier words were still reaching listeners as new words arrived. Making the speaker louder would also make those reflections louder. We needed to change what happened after sound left the speaker.
Interviewer: So are soft surfaces better everywhere? Architect: The right amount depends on the activity. Materials such as thick curtains absorb some sound instead of sending it back into the room. That can make speech clearer. But the music group liked some of the sound that remained after a note. Covering every available surface could take away something those musicians valued. A room used for meetings and music needs choices rather than one permanent setting.
Interviewer: How did you provide those choices? Architect: We hung curtains that can be drawn across several walls for talks and pulled aside for music. We also invited people to listen from different seats. Testing from the stage alone would have missed the original problem. Performers and listeners do not occupy the same position, so their experiences can differ.
Interviewer: What did the project change about your work? Architect: I now ask about the activities before I draw the walls. A beautiful photograph records one view at one moment. It cannot tell me whether a visitor can follow a question from the back row.
q: What is the interview chiefly concerned with?
choices: Choosing a fixed sound setting for public buildings.
Helping speakers overcome a problem with volume.
Designing concert rooms to suit performers alone.
Matching a hall's sound to its various activities.
explain: 各輪問答從語音不清、音樂餘音，到可移動窗簾與不同座位試聽，都談依用途調整。various＝各種的；不是單純音量不足，也不是只考慮表演者的音樂廳。

Passenger update: The Willow village bus will test request stops on its afternoon service for six weeks. At a request stop, the bus stops when someone wants to board or leave; it does not stop merely because the location appears on the route. The market and library will remain regular stops, where the bus stops on every trip. Printed timetables will mark the request stops with the letter R and will remain available from the library desk.
If you are waiting at an R stop, stand where the driver can see you and raise your hand as the bus approaches. If you are already on board, press the bell before your stop. You do not need to explain your journey to the driver. Anyone unsure of the procedure can ask at the library desk before traveling. The trial changes when the bus stops, not where it runs. Fares, the route, and the number of afternoon services will stay the same.
The aim is to avoid unnecessary stops on quiet afternoons while keeping every existing boarding location available. However, a faster journey will not count as a success if passengers find the service harder to use. Drivers will record requests they notice too late, and passengers can report a missed bus using a paper form or by telephone. At the end of the trial, the village will consider both journey times and missed requests. We will revise the instructions or restore regular stops if the new arrangement creates access problems. Please report difficulties as well as praise; an empty complaint box does not necessarily mean an easy journey.
q: What does the announcement mainly explain?
choices: A trial of stops on demand along the same route.
A plan to make the market a stop on demand.
A plan to move quiet stops nearer the library.
A trial requiring paper requests before boarding.
explain: 公告解釋部分站點改成有需求才停，並交代示意、按鈴與評估。on demand＝有需求時；紙本是申訴管道，不是上車申請，市場仍每班停靠。

Monday. Our design class began observing the square between the station and the college. The paved paths made a neat rectangle around a lawn. Across one corner of the grass, however, a narrow strip of bare earth linked the station exit to a college gate. I drew it as damage and suggested a low fence. Our teacher asked us to return at different times before deciding what the mark meant.
Wednesday. In the morning, students crossed the bare strip in a steady stream. At noon, fewer people used it. After a shower, I saw some walkers remain on the pavement even though it took longer. A woman pulling a shopping bag explained that the grass was too soft for its small wheels. The shortcut served a clear purpose, but its usefulness changed with the traveler and the conditions.
Friday. We submitted two drawings. One added a firm path where people had worn the grass away. The other widened an existing corner and gently curved it toward the gate, shortening the paved journey while leaving more lawn together. Neither drawing treated the rectangle as untouchable. Yet neither copied every footprint as an instruction to build. We still needed to consider drainage, maintenance, and users we had not seen during our visits.
My first drawing had shown how to protect a design from people. My final notes asked how the design could learn from them. The bare strip had not supplied a complete plan, but it had revealed a question our tidy rectangle had failed to ask.
q: Which title best reflects the journal's focus?
choices: How a Fence Can Preserve a College Lawn

Why the Paved Paths Are Hard to Maintain
How Students Can Keep a Station Square Tidy
explain: 從把裸土當破壞，到觀察使用需求再提設計，重點是捷徑帶來的啟示。shortcut＝捷徑。圍籬是最初想法，後來已被重新檢討。

A coconut shell lying on a sandy seabed may look like rubbish. For a certain kind of octopus, however, it can become equipment worth taking along. Scientists watching these animals off Indonesia noticed something more interesting than an octopus hiding inside a convenient hole. Some animals collected empty coconut shell halves and carried them across open ground before using them as shelters elsewhere.
Moving the shells involved a cost. An octopus could gather them beneath its body and walk on the tips of its arms, but this was an awkward way to travel. The shells did not protect it during the journey. Only after stopping could the animal arrange its load into a place to hide. Carrying the material therefore made movement harder before it offered any benefit. This delay helped researchers distinguish the behavior from simply occupying a shelter already in place.
The observations widened discussion of animal tool use, which is often associated with birds and mammals. The researchers could record what the animals carried and when they used it, but these actions left questions about their thoughts unanswered. The evidence showed a clear sequence in which an object was transported and later used for protection. Whether the octopuses understood that sequence in the same way humans might remains uncertain. The awkward journey mattered because it separated an immediate physical burden from a benefit that came later.

Why Tool Use Is Often Linked to Birds and Mammals

Our team leader, Nora, asked me to leave the light in the office. Then she took me to the beach without the dramatic rescue equipment I had expected.
From the sand, the restaurant behind us seemed far brighter than it had from the road. Nora explained that newly hatched turtles use patterns of light and darkness to find the sea. On an undeveloped beach, the open ocean horizon is usually brighter than the land. Artificial lights can change that pattern. A row of young turtles might be drawn toward a building instead of the water. I suddenly understood why another bright light was not the simple solution I had imagined.
That night our task was to speak with the restaurant manager. He had already covered the outdoor lamps, but light still escaped through the dining room windows. At Nora's suggestion, he closed the curtains on the beach side. We returned to the sand to check the result from a turtle's height, rather than congratulate ourselves from the road. Later, I helped prepare a note asking guests to keep the curtains closed after dark. I had come hoping to do something visible. By the time I left, I was proud of a change that made the beach harder for people to see.
q: Which change in the narrator best describes the story as a whole?
choices: From seeking a visible role to valuing quiet help
From wanting to guide turtles to wanting to guide guests
From trusting the manager to questioning his cooperation
From admiring the restaurant lights to fearing the sea

Dear Film Team, Thank you for showing our science class an early version of your ocean documentary. The underwater scenes are beautiful, but I have a suggestion about the soundtrack. Whenever the camera moves below the surface, the music stops and silence follows. This creates a peaceful mood, yet it may leave viewers with an inaccurate idea of what the ocean sounds like. I hope your next version will give the underwater world a voice.
The sea has many natural sounds, including waves, rain, and animal calls. A camera may show empty water while an underwater recorder picks up sounds from animals outside the frame. Sound can travel far underwater, so what we hear need not come from what we see. Adding recordings with clear notes about where they were made would help viewers understand this difference. The sounds would carry information rather than simply decorate the images.
Human activity belongs in this sound picture too. Vessel noise can drown out calls that marine animals need to hear. If you turn up a whale's call so it rises clearly above a ship's engine, the film may hide the very problem it discusses. Instead, consider a labeled demonstration: play a call clearly, then let listeners hear how added noise makes it harder to detect. This would be a sound mixture made for teaching, not evidence from a particular encounter. With that distinction explained, the soundtrack could reveal both the richness of ocean sound and the difficulty of hearing within it.
q: Which request is at the center of the letter?
choices: Match each animal call to an animal on the screen.
Use sound to explain the underwater environment.
Make whale calls stand out clearly in noisy scenes.
Use peaceful music to link the underwater sequences.

Tree rings can extend the view into earlier centuries. In trees that form annual rings, each year's growth leaves a layer of wood. The width of that layer reflects growing conditions. Where water is a major limit on growth, repeated dry years may leave a run of narrow rings.
Neither method should be used carelessly. A narrow ring in one tree does not automatically prove a regional drought. Nearby trees may compete for light, and insects can also reduce growth. Researchers therefore compare patterns from many trees and examine how those patterns relate to weather measurements for years covered by both. Agreement across a wider area helps separate a shared climate signal from a problem affecting a particular tree. Knowing the setting matters as much as counting the rings.
Living trees do not set the earliest limit of this approach. Wood from older buildings or fallen trees may preserve patterns that overlap those of living trees. Matching the shared sequence allows researchers to connect shorter records into a longer history. A building beam is useful here not because it contains a description of the weather, but because the tree that became the beam was growing while that weather occurred. Instrument records and tree rings thus contribute different kinds of evidence. Comparing them helps researchers build an account of past drought that reaches beyond the life of a weather station.
q: Which issue organizes the report as a whole?
choices: How different records help reveal earlier droughts
Why old buildings offer better records than forests
How weather stations explain insect damage to trees
Why narrow rings identify trees suited for building

A planting day makes an excellent photograph: volunteers stand beside straight rows of young trees, holding empty pots. The picture records effort, but it cannot tell us whether a forest is returning. If a town wants lasting benefits for wildlife and climate, its restoration budget must follow what happens after the photograph is taken. Counting the trees put into the ground is only the beginning of that task.
Some damaged land still contains young native trees or roots capable of producing new shoots. In such places, helping existing growth may be more useful than filling every space with nursery trees. Workers can protect young plants from repeated fire, reduce pressure from grazing animals, and control grasses that crowd them. These actions give natural recovery a chance to take root. They require skill and regular attention, even when no rows of newly planted trees appear in a photograph.
This approach has limits. If nearby sources of native seeds have disappeared or the land has been badly damaged, planting may be necessary. Choosing between methods requires examining the site, not choosing the activity that draws the largest crowd. The budget should also pay local people for continued care and record how well young trees survive. A smaller planting event followed by years of protection may achieve more than a grand event followed by neglect. We should celebrate volunteers, but the measure of success should be the forest taking shape after they have gone home.
q: Which position does the editorial defend?
choices: Planting more trees should take priority over later care.
Natural recovery should replace planting at damaged sites.
Volunteer numbers should determine restoration budgets.
Lasting recovery should guide restoration spending.
explain: 作者以長期森林復原作為經費標準，restoration 是「復育」。「自然恢復取代植樹」忽略末段指出缺乏種源或受損嚴重時仍須種植。

Ridge Field Meteor Night: The astronomy club invites families to watch a meteor shower from the school field. Meteors are brief flashes of light produced as small pieces of space rock enter the atmosphere. The event begins with an indoor introduction, followed by outdoor viewing if the sky is clear. Unlike the club's planet nights, this event has no telescope stations. Meteors cross broad areas of the sky, so a narrow view through a telescope would make them harder to catch. Bring a folding chair or a blanket and prepare to look up comfortably.
The club has chosen a night when moonlight should cause little interference. Even so, a particular number of meteors cannot be promised. Clouds, local lights, and natural changes in activity all affect what an observer sees. Our poster's picture of several bright streaks combines separate moments; it is not what visitors should expect to see at once. Allow time for your eyes to adjust to the dark, and avoid checking a bright phone screen during viewing. Field lights will remain off, with volunteers guiding arrivals along the marked entrance path.
Registration covers the indoor talk as well as the viewing session. If clouds prevent outdoor observation, the talk will still take place, and visitors will receive a pass for a later viewing evening. Participants who join from home may use the club's live voice channel for comments, but it will not provide a continuous video of the sky. A camera shows only the area toward which it is pointed. The purpose of the channel is to share the experience while each observer watches their own patch of sky.
q: What is the announcement mainly designed to do?
choices: Recruit volunteers to maintain the entrance path
Prepare visitors for the event and what to expect
Teach visitors how to combine photos of the sky
Invite home viewers to watch a shared live sky video
explain: 公告交代活動安排、觀測限制與替代方案，以建立合理 expectation（期待）。「教合成照片」把澄清海報呈現方式的細節當成活動主旨。

Student: Why bring material from an asteroid, a small rocky object orbiting the Sun, back to Earth instead of studying it only with a spacecraft? Laboratory guide: A spacecraft has limited room and power for scientific tools. Back here, researchers can divide a sample among different laboratories and examine it with equipment that could not easily make the journey. They can also keep some material for instruments and questions that do not yet exist.
Student: Once the sample arrives, can we finally stop worrying about it? Guide: Landing is a milestone, not the end of careful handling. Ordinary dust or moisture could change the sample or leave substances that researchers might mistake for part of the asteroid. Controlled work areas and suitable containers help avoid this. For example, nitrogen, a gas that reacts very little with the sample, can protect collected material from contact with oxygen and moisture. The aim is not to make the sample look clean; it is to know what the material was like before Earth's environment could alter it.
Student: Then why not use every grain in the first round of tests? Guide: Some tests consume or permanently change the material they examine. Keeping a portion in reserve leaves future researchers a chance to ask different questions. A result also becomes more useful when another team can check it independently. In that sense, the trip home is only one stage of the mission. The care taken afterward helps decide whether the sample remains a source of discoveries for years or becomes a collection of results that nobody can investigate again.
q: Which idea best summarizes the guide's answers?
choices: Returning samples and caring for them enable lasting study.
Sharing samples quickly matters more than saving material.
Earth laboratories can replace observations made in space.
A clean appearance is the main goal after samples land.
explain: 三段涵蓋帶回的研究優勢、防污染與留樣，lasting 是「長久的」。「地面實驗取代太空觀測」誇大了首段對設備優勢的說明。

Reader's question: If a planet outside our solar system is too faint to appear in a photograph, how can astronomers find it? Answer: They can sometimes watch its star instead. When an orbiting planet crosses the star's face from our point of view, it blocks a small amount of starlight. This crossing is called a transit. Instruments record a temporary decrease in brightness even when the planet itself cannot be seen as a separate point of light.
A single decrease is a clue, not an immediate discovery. A star's own activity or another star passing in front of it can also change the light we receive. Researchers look for repeated decreases with consistent timing and shape, and carry out additional checks before accepting a planet candidate as real. The amount of blocked light can help them estimate the planet's size compared with its star. The time between repeated crossings can reveal how long the planet takes to complete an orbit.
There is a catch: the orbit must line up so the planet crosses the star as seen from Earth. A planet traveling on a differently angled path may never block our view, even if it is large. For that reason, a star with no detected transit should not automatically be labeled a star without planets. This method turns a tiny loss of light into useful information, but it does not provide a complete list of the worlds around every star. To search beyond its limits, astronomers need other methods as well.
q: Which description best captures the answer's main focus?
choices: The differences between the sizes of planets and stars
The equipment needed to obtain images of faint planets
The use and limits of dips in a star's brightness
The effects of orbiting planets on their stars' activity
explain: 全文介紹以星光下降找行星、可得資訊及觀測限制，dip 是「下降」。「行星與恆星大小差異」只是第二段可估算的資訊之一，未涵蓋全文。

When an orbiting planet crosses the star's face from our point of view, it blocks a small amount of starlight. This crossing is called a transit. Instruments record a temporary decrease in brightness even when the planet itself cannot be seen as a separate point of light.
A single decrease is a clue, not an immediate discovery. A star's own activity or another star passing in front of it can also change the light we receive. Researchers look for repeated decreases with consistent timing and shape, and carry out additional checks before accepting a planet candidate as real. The amount of blocked light can help them estimate the planet's size compared with its star. The time between repeated crossings can reveal how long the planet takes to complete an orbit.
There is a catch: the orbit must line up so the planet crosses the star as seen from Earth. A planet traveling on a differently angled path may never block our view, even if it is large. For that reason, a star with no detected transit should not automatically be labeled a star without planets. This method turns a tiny loss of light into useful information, but it does not provide a complete list of the worlds around every star. To search beyond its limits, astronomers need other methods as well.
q: Why can this method miss a large planet even after observing several of its orbits?
choices: Its crossing causes an increase in starlight.
Its path never crosses our view of the star.
Its faintness prevents a separate image of it.
Its size makes the star too bright to measure.
explain: 末段指出軌道角度可使行星始終不遮住視線中的恆星，orbit 是「軌道」。「拍不到行星」誤用直接成像的條件，首段已說此法無須看見行星本體。

A paper straw seems an unlikely invention: paper usually becomes weak when wet. Yet an inventor working in the nineteenth century saw a way to turn that weakness into a manageable problem. Marvin Stone wanted to make an inexpensive substitute for the natural plant tubes then used for drinking. His solution depended on how paper was shaped and protected, rather than on finding a completely new material.
Stone wound a narrow strip of paper around a pencil. The pencil gave the paper a regular shape with a passage through its center. He secured the edge so that the strip would not come loose, then removed the pencil. A coating of wax helped keep liquid from soaking into the paper. Each part of the process answered a separate need: the pencil shaped the tube, the joined edge held it together, and the coating protected it during use. Stone received an American patent for his artificial straw in 1888.
The device also offered control over production. A maker did not have to find a plant stem with exactly the right width; paper could be formed around a chosen guide. Still, a round tube alone was not enough. Without protection from liquid, its useful shape could soon be lost. Stone's work therefore offers a lesson beyond drinking equipment. A familiar material can serve an unexpected purpose when its limitations are addressed through several small decisions working together.
q: Which heading best expresses the central idea of this account?
choices: Choosing Plant Stems for More Reliable Straws
Making Paper Work in a Wet Environment
Making Uniform Tubes: The Whole Solution
Patenting a New Material for Drinking Straws
explain: 全文說明紙如何經成形、固定與防水處理變成吸管。wet environment＝潮溼環境；「均勻成形就是完整解法」忽略末段指出圓管仍須防水。

Trial report: AI notes for the Hill School club council
Our council tested an AI tool that turned meeting recordings into short written summaries. Members had often spent an evening preparing the notes. We hoped the tool would reduce that work while leaving a clear record for students who could not attend. We tested it at two meetings before deciding whether to keep it.
At the first meeting, the tool neatly listed a discussion about holding a concert. However, it reported that the council had approved the event. Members had actually agreed to ask about the hall's cost before making that decision. The summary preserved the exciting proposal but lost its condition. A student who read only the summary began planning ticket sales. No tickets were sold, but correcting the misunderstanding required several messages.
For the second trial, a member announced the final status of each proposal before discussion moved on. Another member checked the resulting summary against those announcements and the recording. Preparing the notes took less time than before the trials, even with this review. The approved version clearly separated decisions from suggestions. We therefore recommend continuing with the tool and keeping a human reviewer. Our comparison covered just two meetings, so the conclusion is tentative. Different speakers or more complicated discussions might create other problems. The useful result was a shorter writing task, provided that someone still took responsibility for the meaning.
q: What is the report chiefly intended to do?
choices: Recommend using a note tool with human review.
Request approval for the proposed school concert.
Recommend replacing written notes with recordings.
Use the trial results to select a concert planning team.
explain: 開頭交代試用，結尾建議保留工具並由人審查。review＝審查；演唱會提案是錯誤摘要的例子，不是報告要申請的事。

Interviewer: Your name appears in books, but you do not write their chapters. What do you do? Lena: I make indexes, the lists of subjects and page numbers at the back. An index gives readers several routes into a book. A contents page follows the order of the chapters; my work follows the questions a reader might bring. Someone looking for a particular idea should not have to guess which chapter contains it.
Interviewer: Why not ask a computer to collect every word and its page number? Lena: Finding words is useful, but ideas can appear without their usual names. A gardening book might explain how to protect roots from freezing without using the word "winter." A reader could still reasonably look under that heading. The reverse problem occurs too: a page may mention winter in passing while offering no useful discussion of it. I must distinguish these cases. A long list of matches can send a reader to many disappointing pages.
Interviewer: How do you choose the headings? Lena: I consider the book's likely readers and connect related terms. If readers might search under different names for the same subject, I can direct them toward a shared entry. That entry is a starting point, not a summary of everything the book says. Before finishing, I check where its page references lead. A polished list is of little use if the reader arrives at a page that merely mentions the topic.
q: Which statement best sums up Lena's contribution to a book?
choices: She changes chapter order to match readers' questions.
She adds explanations missing from the chapters.
She builds routes from readers' ideas to useful pages.
She collects the longest list of words in the text.
explain: 她依讀者問題選詞、串連名稱並檢查頁碼，幫助找到實質內容。route＝途徑；她未改排章節，也非追求詞表最長。
